lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
The fundamental theorem of algebra tells us that any quartic polynomial with real coefficients has precisely four roots.

Content:
Moreover, since complex roots always come in complex conjugate pairs, if [MATH: p(x)] is a quartic polynomial with real coefficients, we must have one of the following cases:

Content:
- [MATH: p(x)] has [MATH: 4] real roots (some of which might be repeated).
- [MATH: p(x)] has [MATH: 2] (possibly repeated) real roots and [MATH: 2] complex conjugate roots. For example,
[MATH: p(x)|= x^{4} − 1; = (x^{2} − 1)(x^{2} + 1); = (x − 1)(x + 1)(x − \textrm{i})(x + \textrm{i}).]
In this case, the real roots are [MATH: x=\pm 1,] and the complex conjugate roots are [MATH: x=\pm\textrm i.]

Content:
- [MATH: p(x)] has two pairs of complex conjugate roots. For example,
[MATH: p(x)|= (x^{2} + 1)(x^{2} + 4); = (x − \textrm{i})(x + \textrm{i})(x − 2\textrm{i})(x + 2\textrm{i}).]
In this case, the complex conjugate pairs of roots are [MATH: x=\pm\textrm i] and [MATH: x=\pm 2\textrm i.]

Also, notice that it's possible for the complex conjugate pairs of roots to be repeated. For example,
[MATH: p(x)|= x^{4} + 2x^{2} + 1; = (x^{2} + 1)^{2}; = ((x − \textrm{i})(x + \textrm{i}))^{2}; = (x − \textrm{i})(x − \textrm{i})(x + \textrm{i})(x + \textrm{i}).]
In this case, the roots are [MATH: x=\pm\textrm i.] Each of these roots is a double root.

Explanation:
Let [MATH: f(x)=x^4 - 6 x^3 + 12 x^2 + 6 x - 13.] Since [MATH: x_1=-1] and [MATH: x_2=1] are roots of [MATH: f(x),] then according to the factor theorem,

[MATH: (x+1)(x-1) = x^2-1]

is a factor of [MATH: f(x).]

Next, we find the quotient when [MATH: f(x)] is divided by [MATH: x^2-1] using polynomial division.
